standard.title: Different Experiences During the Industrial Revolution
standard.description: the different perspectives and experiences of men, women and children during the Industrial Revolution, and their changing way of life
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution (AC9HH9K13) and the population and settlement changes of the period (AC9HH9K015). They have a structural understanding of what industrialisation involved. This descriptor asks them to examine the human experience of those changes — examining how specific groups lived through industrialisation differently depending on class, gender, and age.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine the different perspectives and experiences of men, women and children during the Industrial Revolution, and explain their changing ways of life.

nodes.label: Impact of industrial technologies on daily life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast the impact of steam, gas and electricity on people's way of life during the Industrial Revolution, including differences across social classes.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how one industrial technology (steam, gas, or electricity) changed the daily life of people during the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast the impact of steam, gas and electricity on people's lives during the Industrial Revolution; examine differences in living conditions for rich and poor; describe improvements in living standards for the growing middle class; describe the persistence of poor conditions for the industrial working class; examine changes in working conditions for agricultural workers displaced to factories.
wider: Examine the development of gas lighting in cities and its social effects — examining how artificial light extended working hours and transformed urban social life in ways that benefited different classes differently

Compare the living conditions of factory owners in their new suburban villas with those of mill workers in back-to-back housing in the same city — using contemporary sources such as Charles Booth's poverty maps or Parliamentary reports

response_modes.reason: Class-differentiated analysis is essential here — the same technology (steam, gas, electricity) produced very different experiences depending on where you sat in the economic hierarchy.

success_criteria: Compares the impact of at least one industrial technology on the lives of people from at least two different social positions
Identifies at least one way industrial technology improved living conditions and one way it worsened them for specific groups

nodes.label: Working conditions — adults and children
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the changes in working conditions during the Industrial Revolution, including long hours, low pay, dangerous conditions, and the use of child labour.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two features of working conditions in industrial factories and explain why they developed.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the changes in working conditions including: long hours (12–16 hour days), low and irregular pay, physically dangerous conditions, child labour as a cheap source of labour; describe the specific conditions faced by children in factories and mines; examine primary sources (Parliamentary reports, reformers' accounts) documenting these conditions.
wider: Examine specific Parliamentary reports on child labour (e.g. the Sadler Committee Report, 1832) as primary sources — analysing the testimony of child workers and factory owners to assess how conditions were documented and contested
Compare working conditions in a textile mill with those in a coal mine — examining how different industrial contexts produced different types of risk and exploitation

Investigate the role of women in industrial work — examining how their lower wages than men were justified, what work they did, and how industrial labour both expanded and constrained women's economic roles
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding working conditions — especially for the most vulnerable (children, women, unskilled workers) — is essential for understanding why reform movements (Node 3) emerged and what they were responding to. Without a concrete picture of conditions, trade unions and Factory Acts seem arbitrary rather than responsive.

response_modes.reason: Examining conditions across adult, female, and child workers — and across different industries — prevents a generalised picture and grounds students in the specific circumstances that drove reform.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Working conditions during the Industrial Revolution are documented in rich primary sources — Parliamentary inquiries, reformers' accounts, contemporary illustration — that make the conditions tangible and support genuine source-based historical thinking. The child labour case in particular is historically significant and connects to contemporary child rights debates.
success_criteria: Describes at least three specific features of working conditions in industrial factories or mines
Explains why child labour was widespread and what specific conditions children experienced

nodes.label: Growth of trade unions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the growth of trade unions as a response to the impacts of the Industrial Revolution on the working class and explain how collective action changed the relationship between workers and employers.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what trade unions were and explain why workers formed them during the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the growth of trade unions as a response to poor working conditions and employer exploitation; explain how collective bargaining gave workers leverage they did not have individually; describe key milestones in trade union development; connect trade union growth to the broader reform movement and the Factory Acts.
wider: Examine the Combination Acts (1799, 1800) — which banned trade unions — and their eventual repeal — tracing how workers' collective action was first suppressed and then legally permitted

Investigate the Tolpuddle Martyrs (1834) as a case study in how early trade unionism was criminalised and how the popular response to their transportation changed public attitudes toward workers' rights

Examine the relationship between trade unionism and early socialist ideas — exploring how collective workers' action contributed to the ideological development of socialism as an alternative to capitalism

response_modes.reason: Trade unions integrate the experiences described in Nodes 1–2 with collective political response — students should see union formation as a rational response to specific documented conditions, not as an abstract political phenomenon.

success_criteria: Explains why trade unions grew during the Industrial Revolution, connected to specific working conditions
Describes how collective organisation changed the relationship between workers and employers
